row.note: The commentary sets rain held in rock hollows against vegetation that dries into residue; Psalm 1's tree by irrigation channels bears fruit and does not wither, making lasting nourishment the counterpart to passing debris.

The commentary's Arabic غثاء is flood-borne plant residue that surfaces and disperses; Psalm 1 says the wicked are like chaff the wind drives away, making the discarded plant matter a moral image of what does not endure.
The commentary identifies غثاء as dried vegetation carried off by a flood; Isaiah's grass and flower wither, portraying created vitality as transient and preparing the contrast with what endures.

The commentary pairs a reminder that benefits with the hereafter as more abiding; Isaiah says the grass fades but God's word stands forever, giving divine speech the permanence absent from the residue.
The commentary says a reminder may benefit and defines benefit as help toward good; Moses describes his teaching as rain and dew, making instruction itself life-giving water.

The commentary joins stored water to a reminder that may help people reach good; Isaiah compares God's effective word to rain, saying it does not return empty but accomplishes its purpose, an explicit scriptural bridge from water to beneficial speech.

The commentary includes foam on molten metal among the residue that separates from useful substance; Proverbs says removing dross from silver leaves material for the silversmith's vessel, a refining counterpart to foam departing while value remains.

The commentary's flood carries surface debris that disperses; Isaiah's restless sea casts up mire and mud and cannot rest, using the water's refuse as an image of the wicked, while the surah's foam is what the current leaves behind.

The commentary links its measured wadis to created rock hollows that collect rain; Isaiah asks who measured the waters and marked off the heavens, placing water's bounded order under the Creator's measure.

row.basis: rock becomes pool and flint spring
row.note: The commentary describes God-created hollows in rock that collect rainwater; Psalm 114 says God turns rock into a pool and flint into a spring, adding the reversal in which rock itself becomes a source of provision.

The commentary defines benefit as what helps attain good and sets retained water against useless residue; Hebrews pictures ground drinking repeated rain and producing a useful crop, explicitly joining water with benefit.

The commentary's dried plant matter becomes flood refuse that goes away; Hebrews contrasts useful crop with land bearing thorns and thistles, rejected and ending in fire, giving the unproductive growth an ethical and judgmental outcome.

The commentary moves from God creating and ordering water-holding rock to the hereafter being more abiding; Ecclesiastes says whatever God does endures forever, directly joining divine action and permanence.

The commentary says God knows what is public and what is hidden; Ecclesiastes says God brings every deed, including every hidden thing, into judgment, adding the ethical consequence of divine knowledge.

The commentary calls the hereafter better and more abiding than worldly life; Daniel's resurrection scene distinguishes everlasting life from disgrace, giving a concrete scriptural account of the lasting afterlife.
The commentary calls the hereafter more abiding; Wisdom says the righteous may seem to die but their hope is full of immortality, explaining how apparent loss can conceal a lasting good.

The commentary says the hereafter is better and more abiding; the martyr in 2 Maccabees expects the King of the world to raise the dead to renewed life, placing endurance in bodily resurrection rather than present survival.

The commentary's rock hollows and its explanation of abundant water as water gathered both stress collected water; Genesis makes gathering the waters an act of creation, showing such pools within a larger scriptural ordering of water.

The commentary describes sky-water collected in hollows and links water's benefit to good; Isaiah's rain waters the earth and makes it bring forth seed and bread, supplying the agricultural effect behind its water-and-benefit comparison.

The commentary's dried plant residue belongs to the cycle of pasture becoming waste; Isaiah begins its grass-and-flower comparison by declaring all flesh grass, extending that transience from vegetation to human life.

The commentary distinguishes flood foam that disperses from water that remains; in the psalm's tumultuous scene the waters roar and foam as mountains shake, making foam part of threatening upheaval rather than a sign of useful water.
The commentary says God knows the public and the hidden; the psalm says even darkness is not dark to God, making concealment itself no barrier to divine knowledge.

The commentary makes the benefit of a reminder depend on its helping people reach good and imagines water gathered in hollows; Ta'anit 7a compares Torah to water that descends from high places to low and says Torah endures in the humble, giving receptivity a rabbinic interpretation.

row.basis: water drops wear stone; Torah study
row.note: The commentary imagines rain held in a rock hollow and a beneficial reminder as retained water; Rabbi Akiva's story has drops wear a stone and prompt him to begin Torah study, turning the rock-water meeting into an image of instruction's effect rather than storage.

The commentary compares a beneficial reminder to water held in created rock hollows; Jesus says the one who hears and does his words is like a house built on rock, joining received teaching to stability.

row.basis: rain and flood test the rock house
row.note: The commentary sets water that stays against foam and debris that wash away; Matthew's rain, floods, and winds batter the rock-founded house without bringing it down, making endurance under water the result of doing the teaching.

row.basis: rain and flood collapse the sand house
row.note: The commentary contrasts water retained with transient residue; Matthew's rain and floods collapse the house built on sand, the contrary outcome when the teaching is heard but not done.

The commentary's غثاء is plant residue that disperses and counts for nothing; John gathers wheat into the barn and burns the chaff, making agricultural separation a judgment image of what is kept and what is discarded.

row.basis: water springing up to eternal life
row.note: The commentary connects water held in rock hollows with the hereafter's greater permanence; Jesus says the water he gives becomes a spring welling up to eternal life, joining water's benefit to enduring life.

The commentary describes the hereafter as better and more abiding; Hebrews says its addressees know they possess a better and abiding possession, a close formulation of the same contrast in a persecution context.

The commentary contrasts vanishing foam with the more abiding hereafter; 1 John says the world and its desire pass away while the one doing God's will remains forever, giving the contrast an ethical criterion.

row.basis: seen is transient; unseen is eternal
row.note: The commentary pairs God's knowledge of what is public and hidden with a more abiding hereafter; Paul contrasts visible transient things with unseen eternal things, bringing hiddenness and permanence together.
The commentary says the hereafter is better and more abiding; 1 Peter describes an inheritance kept in heaven as imperishable, undefiled, and unfading, specifying what such permanence means.

row.basis: river of the water of life
row.note: The commentary links water gathered and retained with the lasting hereafter; Revelation's final-city vision has the river of the water of life flowing from God's throne, making life-giving water an eschatological provision.

The commentary defines benefit as help toward good and sets it beside the abiding hereafter; Revelation's tree by the river bears fruit and leaves for the healing of nations, giving the final water scene a concrete benefit.

row.basis: word of the Lord remains forever
row.note: The commentary pairs beneficial reminder with an abiding hereafter; Peter quotes the grass that withers and then says the Lord's word remains forever, applying Isaiah's transience contrast to the proclaimed good news.
The commentary's dried pasture becomes residue that disperses; Peter quotes Isaiah's grass and flower image for all flesh and human glory, extending the fading-vegetation picture to human life.

row.basis: treasure in heaven does not decay
row.note: The commentary says the hereafter is better and more abiding than the transient; Jesus contrasts earthly loss with treasure in heaven that moth and rust cannot consume, making durability a reason to value the future.

row.basis: earthly treasure is destroyed or stolen
row.note: The commentary's foam is what goes while beneficial value remains; Jesus names moth, rust, and thieves as agents that remove earthly treasure, supplying concrete forms of worldly loss against the heavenly treasure in the next verse.

row.basis: the Father sees what is done secretly
row.note: The commentary says God knows what is public and hidden; Jesus says the Father who sees what is done in secret will reward, adding a moral consequence to divine knowledge of concealed acts.
The commentary says God knows what is hidden; Paul says the Lord will bring hidden things to light and disclose heart's purposes, specifying hidden human motives as the object of that knowledge.

row.basis: word held fast and bearing fruit
row.note: The commentary makes reminder beneficial only where it helps toward good and compares it to water held in hollows; Luke's good soil hears the word, holds it fast, and bears fruit with patience, giving reception and retention an ethical outcome.

The commentary asks whether a reminder benefits and defines benefit by help toward good; Paul describes Scripture as useful for teaching, reproof, correction, and training in righteousness, a direct Christian account of beneficial instruction.

The commentary links benefit to reaching good and the hereafter to what is better; Paul says Scripture equips the person of God for every good work, identifying the practical result of useful instruction.

row.basis: flower fades and rich man withers
row.note: The commentary calls the plant residue dried and passing; James likens the rich person to a flower that withers under scorching heat, applying the fading-plant image to worldly prosperity.

The commentary's created rock hollows retain sky-water while flood foam disperses; Jeremiah contrasts the fountain of living water with cisterns unable to hold water, making failed retention an explicit counter-image.

The commentary's source gloss describes cleaning a mud-covered well until clear water appears; Proverbs makes a muddied spring the image of a righteous person yielding to wickedness, giving the same water-clarity image an ethical force.

The commentary joins flood-borne residue to water that remains; Isaiah depicts roaring nations rebuked and chased like chaff before wind, bringing the water-and-disappearing-residue images together in a judgment scene.

The commentary defines benefit as help toward good and describes rain held in rock pools; Ezekiel's river nourishes trees whose fruit feeds and leaves heal, making the water's benefit concrete in an eschatological landscape.
The commentary's well is cleared of mud until its water appears clean; Zechariah's opened fountain cleanses sin and impurity, turning clear water into a specific image of moral purification.

The commentary cites cleaning a well until clear water appears; Elisha goes to Jericho's source and heals its water, so the unusable source becomes sound, a narrative counterpart to water cleared for use.
The commentary's muddy well is cleaned until clear water appears; Ezekiel promises clean water that cleanses Israel from uncleanness, extending the well-clearing image to covenant restoration.

The commentary sets dried pasture against water gathered in hollows; Jeremiah's tree sends roots to water, keeps green leaves through heat and drought, and continues bearing fruit, giving rooted endurance a distinct trust-and-drought setting.

The commentary calls flood-borne plant matter residue that goes away; Hosea compares idolatrous Ephraim to dew that vanishes and chaff swept from the threshing floor, adding transient moisture to the disappearing residue image.

row.basis: water wears stone and washes soil
row.note: The commentary describes rock hollows holding rain and flood matter dispersing; Job reverses the relation as water erodes stone and torrents sweep soil away, setting retained water against destructive runoff.
The commentary includes foam separating from molten metal while useful metal remains; Isaiah's refiner removes Zion's dross and alloy, applying metal separation to the city's moral purification.
The commentary's molten-metal foam separates from what can be used; Malachi depicts a refiner purifying silver and the Levites, giving separation of dross a priestly and ethical interpretation.

The commentary explicitly labels its Arabic branch ر ب ب and glosses it as abundant water named for gathering; Numbers uses Hebrew מַיִם רַבִּים for abundant water gushing from the rock. The matching r-b-b form and water context suggest a cognate, though the source label alone does not establish it.

The commentary distinguishes useless metal foam from the useful metal that remains; Ezekiel calls the house of Israel silver dross in a furnace, reversing the comparison so the community itself is the refuse to be judged.

The commentary's metal image separates passing foam from enduring value; Wisdom says God tests the righteous like gold in a furnace and accepts them, interpreting hardship as refinement rather than waste.

The commentary's metal foam separates from useful material, and its later image distinguishes what vanishes from what remains; Paul says fire tests the quality of each person's work, giving that separation an explicit judgment setting.
The commentary says the hereafter is more abiding and that foam goes while what benefits remains; Paul says the builder whose work remains receives a reward, linking endurance to evaluated work.
The commentary casts the residue as what goes and is not counted; Paul says burned work brings loss, the contrary outcome to work that survives the fire.

row.basis: faith tested as gold by fire
row.note: The commentary invokes metal melted for useful things and contrasts transient residue with lasting good; Peter compares tested faith to gold refined by fire and locates its result at Jesus' appearing.

row.basis: shaken things removed; unshaken things remain
row.note: The commentary's foam goes while water remains and calls the hereafter more abiding; Hebrews says what can be shaken is removed so that what cannot be shaken remains, making permanence the outcome of divine judgment.

row.basis: one spring cannot yield fresh and bitter water
row.note: The commentary's source gloss describes cleaning a well until clear water appears, and it presents reminder as speech that may benefit; James uses spring-water quality to test speech, asking whether one opening can yield both fresh and bitter water.
